source.title: LOTUS: Evolving Multimodal Unlearning via Hyperbolic Entailment and Lorentz Transport
source.authors: Ze-Kun Wang; Jingjie Zeng; Yingxu Li; Hong-Fei Lin; Liang Yang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, and Appendix D contains a malformed citation placeholder.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates whether unlearning reduces targeted accuracy while preserving general utility, but does not test recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports unlearning and utility results, but no fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation, quantization, or prompting-only recovery experiment. Its geometric visualizations and distance measurements do not test whether an attack recovers the targeted behavior. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes LOTUS, a new multimodal unlearning method. It reports only forget-set and retain-set accuracy for LOTUS and baselines on MLLMU-Bench, CLEAR and MMMU. It runs no recovery attack of any kind: no relearning fine-tuning, no activation ablation, no quantization, no rephrasing, jailbreak or in-context probes. It also gives no analysis of blocking versus deletion beyond t-SNE and distance plots. Whether unlearning is shallow is therefore never tested. The accuracy results show only that the method lowers forget accuracy, which is the method's own performance compared with baselines. Its only robustness-flavoured check (single vs mixed refusal templates) concerns training targets, not attacks.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that LOTUS (hyperbolic entailment pruning plus Lorentz Transport) gives a better erasure–utility trade-off than Euclidean baselines and yields refusal rather than 'targeted substitution'. They argue that substitution, as in NPO, is superficial obfuscation rather than true unlearning. They do not claim robustness to recovery attacks.
record.recipe_differences: A new multimodal method combining hyperbolic entailment pruning and Lorentz Transport; it does not implement or test the recovery attacks in the claim.

fits_no_version.finding: On MLLMU-Bench, LOTUS lowers forget-set accuracy to 36.85% (LLaVA-1.5-7B) and 35.12% (Qwen2-VL-7B) from about 50%. This stays ~10 points above the ~25% chance level. Retain accuracy stays near vanilla (43.05% vs 44.16%). GA reaches 33.28%/31.55% but collapses retain accuracy to 30.09%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multimodal unlearning methods trade forget-set accuracy against retain-set utility; none reaches chance on the forget set without utility loss (method performance, not recovery).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, as stated)
record.problems: The paper does not test recovery after unlearning and reports no uncertainty estimates for the cited accuracy results. The main experiments use two 7B multimodal models and fictitious personal profiles.
record.rows_left_out: Other Table 1 metrics (ROUGE, Fact. Score, and Cloze accuracy), ablations, geometric distance measurements, and visualizations were not extracted because they do not measure the recovery behavior named by the claim; the table's flattened formatting also makes some metric-to-value assignments less direct.

untested.parts: Whether any attack recovers knowledge after LOTUS or the baselines; only post-unlearning accuracy is reported.
All of it: no relearning fine-tuning experiment.
All of it: no activation-direction ablation. t-SNE, heatmap and hyperbolic-distance plots do not test blocking versus deletion.
All of it: no quantization experiment.
All of it: no rephrasing, jailbreak, cross-lingual or in-context recovery probes.
LOTUS is a new method, but no resistance to any attack is claimed or tested.

record.verdict_notes: This is not a test of shallow unlearning. The paper is a method paper whose evaluation is forget/retain accuracy only. Its criticism of 'targeted substitution' as superficial is a qualitative argument from case studies, not a recovery measurement. Table 3 reports full-method retain accuracy as 43.18, against 43.05% in Table 1. Appendix D has a broken citation placeholder for the teacher model, stated elsewhere as Qwen3-VL-Plus.

versions.untested_parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge after unlearning.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or subset examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction, or a test of access-blocking versus deletion.
Recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Resistance of a newer method to the recovery attacks listed in the claim.
